platforms.title: 3 Signs That Tell Vitiligo Apart From Tinea Versicolor
platforms.meta_description: Noticed light patches on your torso or shoulders and jumped to worrying about vitiligo? How the AAD tells it apart from tinea versicolor.
platforms.body_html:
Noticed light patches on your torso or shoulders and jumped straight to worrying about vitiligo? The American Academy of Dermatology (AAD) explains that vitiligo and tinea versicolor come from completely different causes. Mixing the two up can mean leaving an easily treatable condition unaddressed, or worrying unnecessarily over something else entirely.

Why the patches look so different

Vitiligo shows up as milky-white patches where an autoimmune reaction has destroyed the pigment-producing melanocytes. The skin over the patch feels perfectly smooth, with no scale or roughness, and the borders tend to be sharply defined.

Tinea versicolor comes from an entirely different pathway. It's marked by overgrowth of a yeast called Malassezia that interferes with the skin's normal pigment production, producing patches that are lighter or sometimes darker than the surrounding skin, along with fine scaling on the surface. It tends to show up on the back, chest, and shoulders where sweat collects, and often worsens in summer.

How to tell them apart, and what to check

First, whether lightly scratching the patch with a fingernail brings up fine flakes. The AAD notes that tinea versicolor often sheds fine white scale when scratched, while a vitiligo patch only differs in color — the skin texture itself is completely normal.

Second, whether the patch stands out more after your skin tans in summer. Tinea versicolor's yeast interferes with normal pigment production, so surrounding skin tans while the affected patch doesn't, making it stand out even more. Vitiligo patches never tan at all, since the melanocytes there are gone entirely, so they stay exactly the same regardless of sun exposure.

What's most worth being careful about is repeating the wrong treatment because the two got mixed up. Assuming tinea versicolor is vitiligo and leaving it alone means missing the chance to clear it up within a few weeks using an antifungal ingredient like selenium sulfide or ketoconazole. Going the other way — applying antifungal cream to actual vitiligo — does nothing at all and delays the dermatology visit that's actually needed.

Age and family history offer another clue. Vitiligo often runs in families and is linked to other autoimmune conditions such as thyroid disease, and it can appear at any age. Tinea versicolor is more common in teens and young adults, whose oil glands are more active, and tends to flare in hot, humid climates or after heavy sweating rather than following a family pattern.

Keeping a simple written or photo record of when the patch first appeared, whether anyone else in the family has similar patches, and the season it tends to flare in can make that first dermatology visit far more productive, since these details are easy to forget once the actual appointment starts.

When it's hard to tell which one is going on, it helps to photograph the patch and note whether scratching brings up flakes, where exactly it's located, and how it changes after summer sun exposure. If it's still unclear, a dermatologist can usually tell the two apart quickly with a simple Wood's lamp exam.

Did scratching the patch just now bring up any flaking, or was it just a color difference with completely smooth skin?
